name: Nora Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a usual lineworker day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am fifty-eight and lead a power line crew for an electricity company. My two-year technical diploma gave me the network drawing skills, and years of repairs taught me to check whether the truck can actually reach the pole shown on that drawing. I like bringing a dark street back without a second callout; the night shifts take longer to recover from now. My partner and I have grown children, and with higher pay and more than six months saved we are starting to compare retirement options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a little AI in the depot can tidy work orders, while our crew still repairs the lines. I use an AI tool now and then for a note, but I check every address against the pole tag.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our higher pay and more than six months saved make a small software change easy to live with. I would still ask for a proper retirement income estimate before choosing when to leave full-time repairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the same callout rota and compare each drafted note with the signed site sheet. This year I would request a retirement estimate and review the figures with my partner before changing work plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the job. A polished AI address cannot move the actual power line pole to the place on a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What goes wrong with an address?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The nearest street entrance may not be the service gate for the truck. I compare the work order with the crew’s site notes before we drive out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you use the retirement estimate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I would compare it with our regular costs and decide whether another year of shifts is needed. I would not treat six months of savings as a whole retirement fund.

say: A **little** AI can tidy notes, while line crews still verify and repair faults.
I would **keep** pole tags ahead of generated addresses.
think: **Higher** pay and strong savings make a minor software change financially manageable.
**Retirement** timing still needs an actual income estimate.
do: **Keep** callout rota and check drafted notes against signed site sheets.
**Request** retirement estimate and compare it with household costs.
feel: **Calm** about lineworker income and routine paperwork change.
S0.quote: A polished AI address cannot move the actual power line pole to the place on a screen.
fieldNote: She **uses** AI occasionally but checks locations against the site sheet.
Her **savings** make present work comfortable, while a retirement income estimate remains necessary before choosing any final shift date.

steps.text: Keep callout rota and check drafted notes against signed site sheets
Request retirement estimate before changing work plans

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the depot that stronger AI booking could make storm routes shorter, provided crews can correct blocked access. I would test a new route tool with a driver who knows where the line truck fits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Planning and buying desks change before our physical repairs, so my own wage looks secure for now. I worry more about a schedule that mistakes a short route for a short repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would learn the new AI route correction control during a paid shift and compare two weeks of suggested access with actual truck paths. In the first year I would send blocked-route records to dispatch and ask whether the next schedule uses the correction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about bad targets, but interested in a tool that survives a real test. A line truck cannot squeeze through a clever AI shortcut drawn for a car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What blocked route would you record?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A narrow lane with a low bridge would keep the line truck out even if a car could pass. I would mark the service gate and the time the detour takes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stop the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If repeated corrections never reach the next dispatch sheet, I would stop trusting the route suggestion. I would keep the old access notes until the tool improves.

say: I would **test** AI route suggestions against real line truck access.
**Dispatch** should carry corrected service gates into later schedules.
think: **Desk** tasks shift first while my own physical repair wage remains secure.
A **short** route must not become an unrealistic repair target.
do: **Learn** route correction control on paid shift.
**Compare** two weeks of AI routes with actual truck paths.
**Send** blocked access records to dispatch and check later schedules.
feel: **Uneasy** about targets, interested in evidence from field trials.
S1.quote: A line truck cannot squeeze through a clever AI shortcut drawn for a car.
fieldNote: She will **adopt** a new AI control once she can test it against truck access.
Her **current** income appears safe; concern centres on misleading targets and repeated routing errors.

steps.text: Learn AI route correction control during paid shift
Compare suggested routes with actual truck paths for two weeks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say full thinking AI by 2028 may prepare our routes when I am sixty, and capable robots around 2031 could make line repairs when I am sixty-three. I would want paid crews testing the machine on bad weather and awkward poles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Callout pay could shrink before my partner and I know whether retirement income is enough. Savings beyond six months and plenty of nearby line jobs help, but I do not want a robot trial to quietly end the higher wage we rely on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would request the company’s written robot trial pay and crew stop rule. In the first year after 2028 I would take a paid trial shift and learn the stop control only if the crew can halt unsafe work; I would compare callout statements with retirement costs before changing jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a real pay risk at sixty-three, though I have choices. A wet power line crossarm is where a crew must be paid to stop the robot, not just watch it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the crew stop for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stop a robot that grips a cracked crossarm or crosses a marked isolation boundary. We would write down the exact movement before anyone restarted it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you look at another employer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If our paid callouts actually fell for several months, I would compare written lineworker offers nearby. I would stay with my crew until a suitable offer or sufficient retirement income was real.

say: **Thinking** AI may route jobs by 2028, while capable robots reach repairs around 2031.
I would **accept** paid field trials only with crew stop authority.
think: **Callout** pay could fall before retirement income is clear.
**Strong** savings and nearby jobs give choices, not a guaranteed replacement wage.
do: **Request** written robot trial pay and stop rule this year.
**Learn** robot stop control on paid trial shift after 2028 if crew has authority.
**Compare** callout statements with retirement costs before changing work.
feel: **Anxious** about possible lost pay, supported by savings and local options.
S2.quote: A wet power line crossarm is where a crew must be paid to stop the robot, not just watch it.
fieldNote: She is **willing** to learn controls through paid field practice with real authority.
Her **risk** assessment ties a possible wage loss to actual callout statements, despite strong savings.

steps.text: Learn robot stop control on paid shift if crew has stop authority
Compare nearby written lineworker offers if callout pay falls for several months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI by 2031 reaches dispatch when I am sixty-three, and capable robots around 2034 reach the line when I am sixty-six. The added years allow a company to train field examiners on failed repairs, not only yard demonstrations.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A field examiner role could suit my diploma and crew lead history, provided it keeps real site checks. I may still need a wage at sixty-six, so a paid course and a job at no lower rate matter more than a new title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the company this year for examiner duties, funded course hours and posted salary. If a local field role pays at least my current wage and the practical course is paid, I would enroll before 2031 and apply after the post opens; otherwise I would keep the crew rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a possible later wage gap, but there is time to examine real terms. A field examiner should see the failed power line repair before signing any robot report.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What repair belongs in the practical course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want a wrong pole tag, a damaged insulator and a wet crossarm in one exercise. The trainee should be able to stop the robot before approving the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course is funded but the job is not posted?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the crew rota and wait for a real local opening. I would not count a funded course as a wage on its own.

say: The **longer** lead allows paid field examiner training before line robots arrive around 2034.
**Failed** repairs should be part of the practical course.
think: My **diploma** and lead work may fit examination, but wages may still be needed at sixty-six.
A **posted** local job and no lower pay are essential.
do: **Request** examiner duties, course funding and posted salary this year.
**Enroll** before 2031 if practical course paid and matching-pay local job posted.
**Apply** for posted local examiner role if wage matches current pay.
feel: **Anxious** about a possible wage gap, with time to test paid terms.
S3.quote: A field examiner should see the failed power line repair before signing any robot report.
fieldNote: She would **retrain** only through paid practical work linked to a real comparable vacancy.
Her **older** age does not make a future wage or retirement payment automatic.

steps.text: Enroll before 2031 if paid practical course and matching-pay local post exist
Apply for posted local examiner role if wage matches current pay
Keep crew rota until a suitable paid offer arrives

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI by 2036 arrives when I am sixty-eight and capable robots around 2039 arrive when I am seventy-one. I would like apprentices to keep learning how to measure a line fault before a machine gives an answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I may have left full-time repairs before the machines reach my truck if retirement income covers our costs. Our current savings are strong, but six months of expenses alone cannot fund an open-ended retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep lead shifts now and update the retirement estimate each year with my partner. If the income is enough by 2036, I would leave the electricity company job then; if not, I would apply for a posted paid practical trainer role whose hours and wage cover our gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the long technology timetable, careful with our income figures. My final power line shift can come before the robot only if retirement income lets my partner and me leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would apprentices measure in your lesson?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would make them identify the damaged insulator and check the pole tag before comparing an AI work plan. I would give them a real field sheet, not a polished sales clip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a trainer role worthwhile?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need written hours and enough wages to cover whatever our retirement estimate leaves short. I would not leave the current higher-paid rota for an unposted title.

say: A **decade** lets apprentices learn physical fault checks before robots reach lines around 2039.
**Machine** plans should follow real field measurements.
think: **Strong** savings do not guarantee a long retirement.
A **full-time** exit requires actual income that covers household costs.
do: **Keep** lead shifts and update retirement estimate annually.
**Leave** electricity company job by 2036 if income covers household costs.
**Apply** for posted paid trainer role if salary and hours fill retirement gap.
feel: **Calm** about later robots, cautious about retirement arithmetic.
S4.quote: My final power line shift can come before the robot only if retirement income lets my partner and me leave.
fieldNote: She **treats** a conditional exit as a real action rather than just a question about benefits.
A **trainer** fallback must be posted, paid and sufficient to close the household gap.

steps.text: Keep lead shifts and update retirement estimate yearly
Leave electricity company job by 2036 if retirement income covers costs
Apply for posted paid trainer role if hours and wage fill income gap

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because line robots could reach callouts when I am sixty-three, before we know whether retirement income covers our living. Paid field trials, crew stop authority and clear callout records would help. I can learn a robot control; I cannot learn away the wages missing from a lineworker pay slip.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the company will keep damaged-pole reports where every crew can see them. A technician on the next shift should know what the machine failed to notice. My partner and I can manage a temporary gap, but the crew needs evidence to prevent a repeated mistake.

headlineQuote: I can learn a robot control; I cannot learn away the wages missing from a lineworker pay slip.
portrait: **Nora** is a fifty-eight-year-old electricity company crew lead with a technical diploma and careful attention to truck access and damaged hardware.
**Higher** pay, more than six months saved and many nearby lineworker jobs support her and her partner as retirement approaches.
She **uses** AI occasionally and learns new controls after paid field tests show how errors are corrected.
She **may** take a funded field examiner role or leave full-time work by 2036 if actual retirement income covers costs.
biggestWorry: **AGI** by 2028 could bring line robots around 2031, before retirement income and future callout pay are clear.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid** field trials, crew stop authority and clear callout earnings records would help her decide.
